analogy.p: Imagine a very crowded classroom next to an empty corridor. Everyone is walking about randomly, but because there are far more people near the door on the classroom side, more people wander out into the corridor than wander back in. Eventually the people are spread out evenly and, although everyone still moves about, there is no overall flow: that is **equilibrium**. A wider door (larger surface area) lets more people through, a hurried crowd (higher temperature) moves faster, and a very full room compared with an empty corridor (steeper gradient) gives the quickest flow. The analogy breaks down because people can choose where to go and may avoid each other, whereas particles move completely randomly and without any 'wanting' to leave.
analogy.t: A crowded room with an open door

bullets: Say '**net movement from a higher to a lower concentration**' (or 'down a concentration gradient') to gain the mark.
It applies to **gas particles** (e.g. oxygen, carbon dioxide) and particles **in solution** (e.g. urea, glucose).
It is a **passive** process: it does **not need energy from respiration**.
The difference in concentration between two regions is called the **concentration gradient** (a steeper gradient means a bigger difference).
Movement 'down' the gradient means from high to low; movement 'against' the gradient (low to high) needs **active transport** instead.
Do not write that particles 'want' to move or are 'attracted' to low concentration; they move randomly.
core.h: The definition to learn word for word
core.p: **Diffusion** is the **spreading out of the particles of any substance in solution, or particles of a gas, resulting in a net movement from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration**. The key phrase is **net movement**: particles move in all directions, but more move from the crowded region than into it, so overall they spread out. Diffusion happens in gases and in solutions, but not in solids because the particles cannot move freely.

bullets: Particles move **randomly** in all directions because of their kinetic energy.
More particles are present where the concentration is high, so **more leave than arrive**.
At **equilibrium** the concentration is the same everywhere and there is no net movement, but individual particles still move.
The rate of diffusion is **fastest at the start** (steepest gradient) and slows as the gradient falls.
On a graph of concentration against time, the curve is steep at first and then **levels off**.
A drop of dye in water or the smell of perfume spreading through a room shows diffusion in a liquid and a gas.
core.h: Why diffusion happens: random particle motion
core.p: All particles in gases and liquids are constantly moving randomly because they have **kinetic energy**. In a region of high concentration there are more particles, so more of them happen to move towards the low concentration region than the other way. This produces a **net movement down the concentration gradient**. When concentrations become equal, particles still move randomly but there is **no net movement**: this is **equilibrium** (dynamic equilibrium).

bullets: Membranes are **partially (selectively) permeable**.
**Small** molecules can diffuse through; **large** molecules cannot.
No energy from respiration is needed, so diffusion is a **passive** process.
The direction depends only on the concentration gradient: from high to low concentration.
Substances can diffuse **into** or **out of** a cell depending on which side has the higher concentration.
Link: diffusion of water has a special name, **osmosis** (next topic); movement against the gradient needs energy (active transport).
core.p: Cell membranes are **partially permeable**: they let some substances through but not others. Small molecules such as **oxygen, carbon dioxide, water and urea** can diffuse through, but large molecules such as starch and proteins cannot. For diffusion to occur across a membrane, there must be a concentration gradient and the particles must be small enough to pass through. The membrane does not need to do any work, so this is a passive process.

bullets: **Oxygen and carbon dioxide** are exchanged in **gas exchange** (lungs, leaves, gills).
**Urea** diffuses from body cells **into the blood plasma** for excretion by the **kidney**.
In respiring tissues, oxygen is used up, so its concentration is low inside the cell and oxygen diffuses in; CO2 is made, so it diffuses out.
In a leaf, CO2 is used in photosynthesis so its concentration falls inside, and CO2 diffuses in through the stomata.
Digested food molecules (glucose, amino acids) can also diffuse from the small intestine into the blood (link to villi).
Always say which way the substance moves and why: 'from a higher to a lower concentration'.
core.p: AQA lists three examples. **Oxygen** diffuses into cells (e.g. from the blood into respiring cells, and from the air into the blood in the lungs). **Carbon dioxide** diffuses out of cells into the blood and from the blood into the lungs, and in plants CO2 diffuses into leaves for photosynthesis. **Urea**, a waste product of protein breakdown, diffuses from cells into the **blood plasma**, and is then carried to the **kidneys** to be excreted in urine.

bullets: Bigger concentration difference means a **faster** rate of net movement.
Rate falls as the concentration difference decreases and stops at equilibrium.
Organisms maintain steep gradients by **ventilation** (breathing moves fresh air in) and a **good blood supply** (which carries the substance away).
If the gradient is doubled, the rate is roughly doubled (directly proportional).
Exam phrase: 'a steeper concentration gradient increases the rate of diffusion because more particles move from the high concentration area than the low'.
Keeping the outside concentration high and the inside low gives the steepest gradient.
core.p: The greater the **difference in concentration** (steeper concentration gradient), the **faster** the rate of diffusion. This is because many more particles move from the high concentration region than the other way, so the net movement is larger. As diffusion proceeds the gradient falls, so the rate slows. Living things keep the gradient steep by removing the diffused substance (for example, blood carries oxygen away from the lungs).

bullets: Higher temperature gives particles more **kinetic energy**.
Particles **move faster**, so the rate of net movement increases.
Cold conditions slow diffusion (e.g. cold-blooded animals are less active in the cold).
Warm-blooded animals keep a constant body temperature so diffusion rate is steady.
In a graph, rate increases as temperature increases (curve rising upwards).
Very high temperatures can denature proteins in cell membranes, which would damage the membrane.
core.p: A higher **temperature** increases the rate of diffusion. At higher temperatures particles have more **kinetic energy**, so they move faster and collide more often, spreading out more quickly. Do not say particles 'gain energy so they move more' without linking this to faster movement and more movement across the membrane. In living organisms the effect is limited because very high temperatures damage enzymes and proteins in the membrane.

bullets: More surface area means **more space for particles to cross** per second.
Exchange surfaces are **folded** or have **projections** to increase surface area.
Examples: **alveoli** in lungs, **villi** in the small intestine, **root hair cells**, **gills** with many filaments.
A cell with a larger surface area compared with its volume diffuses substances in and out more efficiently.
The rate is directly proportional to surface area if other factors are constant.
Link: this leads to surface area to volume ratio (next spec point).
core.h: Factor 3: surface area of the membrane
core.p: The **larger the surface area** of the membrane, the **faster** the rate of diffusion, because more particles can cross at the same time. This is why exchange surfaces are folded or have many tiny projections (alveoli, villi). Doubling the area approximately doubles the number of particles that can pass in a given time.

bullets: Shorter diffusion distance means a **faster** rate of diffusion.
Alveoli and capillary walls are **one cell thick**, giving a very short pathway.
A thick barrier slows diffusion because particles take longer to cross.
Exchange surfaces are thin to make diffusion **quick and efficient**.
In exam answers, mention the 'short diffusion pathway' or 'thin membrane' explicitly.
Remember the four adaptations: large surface area, thin membrane, good blood supply (animals), ventilation (gas exchange).
core.h: Other factors: membrane thickness and diffusion distance
core.p: Although AQA only lists three factors, you should also know that a **thinner membrane** (a shorter **diffusion distance**) makes diffusion faster. Particles have less distance to travel. This is why exchange surfaces such as alveoli walls are only **one cell thick**. Together with surface area and concentration gradient this is a key part of the answer to 'how is this exchange surface adapted?'.

bullets: Small cells have a **large surface area to volume ratio**.
The **diffusion distance** from the surface to the centre is short.
Enough oxygen and nutrients can diffuse in, and waste out, to meet the cell's needs.
So no specialised transport or exchange systems are needed.
Exam phrase: 'single-celled organisms have a large surface area to volume ratio so diffusion alone can supply their needs'.
Contrast with multicellular organisms below.
core.p: A **single-celled organism** has a **relatively large surface area to volume ratio**. This means that substances only have a very short distance to diffuse and there is a large surface for them to enter through compared with the volume of cell needing supplying. Therefore diffusion across the cell membrane is enough to transport molecules into and out of the cell to meet the needs of the organism. Amoeba is a typical example.

bullets: Small surface area to volume ratio compared with single-celled organisms.
Cells in the **centre** are far from the surface, so diffusion alone is **too slow**.
Need **specialised exchange surfaces** (lungs, small intestine, gills, leaf).
Need a **transport system** (blood in animals, xylem and phloem in plants).
The transport system carries substances to and from exchange surfaces so a steep gradient is kept.
Higher tier link: you may be asked to explain using numerical surface area to volume ratios.
core.h: Multicellular organisms: why diffusion alone is not enough
core.p: A **multicellular organism** has a **smaller surface area to volume ratio** because it is much bigger. The surface area does not increase as quickly as the volume, and many cells are deep inside the body, far from the surface. Diffusion over such a long distance would be too slow to supply all cells with oxygen and remove waste. Therefore multicellular organisms need **specialised exchange surfaces** and a **transport system** (such as the circulatory system) to carry materials around the body.

bullets: **Large surface area** (folds, villi, alveoli, many gill filaments).
**Thin membrane / short diffusion path** (often one cell thick).
**Efficient blood supply** to carry substances away and keep the concentration gradient steep (animals).
**Ventilation** to bring fresh air or water to the surface in gas exchange.
Examples: alveoli (lungs), villi (small intestine), gills (fish), root hair cells, leaf (stomata and air spaces).
Always link feature to function: 'large surface area so more diffusion'.
core.p: Exchange surfaces are organs or tissues adapted to make diffusion **fast and efficient**. AQA says they have: a **membrane that is thin**, so there is a short diffusion path; a **large surface area** (e.g. folded membranes); **efficient blood supply** (in animals) to maintain a steep gradient; and in gas exchange surfaces, being **ventilated** (air moves in and out). You will see these again in the lungs, small intestine, gills and plants.

bullets: Rate = amount diffused (change in concentration) ÷ time taken.
Steeper line on a graph = faster rate; levelling off = equilibrium reached.
Practical: investigate the effect of temperature on diffusion of dye or colour change in agar.
Control variables: volume and concentration of solutions, size of agar pieces, time, temperature (unless it is the independent variable).
Use a **ruler** or timer, repeat to find a **mean**, and identify anomalies.
Higher tier: use a tangent to calculate the rate at a point on a curved graph.
core.p: A common practical uses agar jelly containing indicator to model diffusion, or coloured dye in water at different temperatures. Data questions usually ask you to calculate a **rate** (change divided by time) or describe a graph. On a concentration-time graph, a steeper line means a faster rate, and a flat line means equilibrium. At Higher tier you can find the rate at one point by drawing a **tangent** to the curve and calculating its gradient.

bullets: **Diffusion**: passive, down a gradient, any particles.
**Osmosis**: passive, net movement of **water** across a partially permeable membrane from dilute to concentrated solution.
**Active transport**: uses **energy** from respiration to move substances **against** the concentration gradient.
Surface area to volume ratio explains why organisms have exchange surfaces.
Gas exchange: oxygen diffuses into blood, CO2 diffuses out into alveoli.
Urea is made in the liver, diffuses into blood plasma, and is excreted in urine by the kidney.
core.p: Diffusion is essential across Paper 1 biology. It links to **osmosis** and **active transport** (other transport methods), **gas exchange** in lungs and leaves, **digestion and absorption** in villi, **photosynthesis** (CO2 in), **respiration** (O2 in), and the **kidney** (urea). Comparing diffusion with osmosis and active transport is a standard exam question.

exam: **Define diffusion (2 marks)**: 'spreading out of particles' + '**net movement** from higher to lower concentration'.
**Name/Give (1 mark)**: e.g. one substance that diffuses: oxygen, carbon dioxide or urea.
**Factors (2-3 marks)**: name the factor, say the rate increases, and explain why (steeper gradient, more kinetic energy, more surface area).
**Calculation (2-3 marks)**: rate = change ÷ time; show working and give units (e.g. arbitrary units per minute).
**Explain why large organisms need exchange surfaces (4 marks)**: small SA:V, long diffusion distance, diffusion too slow, need specialised exchange surfaces and transport system.
**Adaptations (3-4 marks)**: pair each feature with its function: large surface area, thin membrane, blood supply, ventilation.
**Graph questions**: describe the shape (steep then levelling off), quote data with units, and explain it using the concentration gradient.
**Compare diffusion with osmosis and active transport**: passive/needs energy, direction relative to gradient, what is moved.
**Required phrase**: 'down a concentration gradient' or 'from a higher to a lower concentration'.
Do not just repeat the question; always add a 'because' reason for explain questions.
For practical questions: independent, dependent and control variables, and ways to improve reliability (repeats, mean).

mistakes.r: Use '**net movement** from a **higher to a lower concentration**'; particles move randomly.
mistakes.w: Diffusion is when particles move from high to low concentration.

mistakes.r: Diffusion is **passive**: no energy from respiration is needed.
They keep moving, but there is **no net movement**.
Higher temperature gives particles more **kinetic energy**, so they move **faster**.
mistakes.w: Higher temperature makes particles bigger / makes membrane open.

mistakes.r: They need it, but a **large surface area to volume ratio** means **diffusion is enough**.
mistakes.w: Single-celled organisms do not need oxygen.

mistakes.r: **Diffusion distance is too long** and surface area to volume ratio too small, so they need **exchange surfaces and transport systems**.
mistakes.w: Big organisms use diffusion because it is quick.

mistakes.r: A thin membrane gives a **short diffusion path**, so diffusion is faster.
mistakes.w: Exchange surfaces are thin 'so things can get through'.

mistakes.r: Osmosis is the diffusion of **water** across a **partially permeable membrane**.
mistakes.w: Osmosis and diffusion are the same thing.

mistakes.r: Active transport is **against** the gradient and **needs energy**.
mistakes.w: Active transport is down the concentration gradient.

summary: AQA wants you to define **diffusion** as the spreading out of particles resulting in a **net movement from a higher to a lower concentration**, give biological examples (oxygen, carbon dioxide, urea), and explain how **concentration difference, temperature and surface area** change its rate. You must also link diffusion to **surface area to volume ratio**, explaining why single-celled organisms can rely on it but multicellular organisms need **exchange surfaces** and transport systems.

At equilibrium both sides have the same concentration; particles still move randomly but there is no net movement. The process is passive, so it needs no energy from respiration.

svg.cap: Diffusion across a cell membrane in a respiring cell. Oxygen is at higher concentration outside and diffuses in; carbon dioxide and urea are made in the cell, so they diffuse out into the blood plasma (urea is then carried to the kidney). The membrane is partially permeable: small molecules cross but large molecules such as proteins cannot.

worked.q: The concentration of oxygen inside a cell increases from 12 to 36 arbitrary units in 6 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of diffusion of oxygen into the cell. (2 marks)

worked.ans: An amoeba is a single-celled organism with a **large surface area to volume ratio**, so substances only diffuse a short distance and **diffusion alone meets its needs**. A human has a **much smaller surface area to volume ratio** and many cells are deep inside the body, so the **diffusion distance is too long** and too slow. Humans therefore need **specialised exchange surfaces** (e.g. alveoli) and a **transport system** (blood) to supply all cells.
worked.q: Explain why a large multicellular organism such as a human needs specialised exchange surfaces but an amoeba does not. (4 marks)
steps: Amoeba: large surface area to volume ratio and short diffusion distance, so diffusion across the membrane is enough.
Human: small surface area to volume ratio; many cells are far from the surface.
Diffusion would be too slow over this distance.
So specialised exchange surfaces and a transport system (blood) are needed.

worked.ans: During exercise the muscle cell respires faster, using oxygen so its concentration inside the cell is lower, while the blood supply keeps the oxygen concentration outside high. This makes the **concentration gradient steeper**, so oxygen diffuses into the cell **faster**.
worked.q: Explain why the rate of diffusion of oxygen into a muscle cell increases during exercise. (3 marks)
steps: The cell respires faster and uses up oxygen, so the concentration inside the cell falls.
Blood brings more oxygen, keeping the outside concentration high.
The concentration gradient is steeper, so the rate of diffusion increases.
